item.title: Does Your Mindset Get in Your Way?
item.description:
Growth Mindset

Does Your Mindset Get in Your Way?

How to cultivate a better mindset. Be open 开放.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Growth can get stifled when we feel vulnerable or shut off.
  • If we cling to defeatist thinking, we are unlikely to push through life’s obstacles.
  • But a nimble sensibility can help bypass closed doors and see the open ones. We are open 开放.
Source: AI-Assisted

The growth mindset sees mistakes and failures as opportunities for learning, and criticism as constructive feedback, not personal attacks. People with a growth mindset embrace imperfection and feel it’s fine to be flawed and altogether average. For them, engaging in the process is more important than the outcome. For them, being knee-deep in an undertaking is the whole point. They do not have to rush or be the first to finish. Instead, they take their time and are okay with their slow but steady progress.

My father was a good example of someone with a healthy growth mindset. In his youth, he discovered he was good at studying and test-taking. When various wealthy families in the neighborhood heard about this, they ordered him to take exams for their sons. Dad agreed to do this to avoid a broken nose and being beaten up. At the root of Dad’s success: Curiosity. He taught himself to do many things. He learned, through reading, how to ride a horse, shoot a gun, play the harmonica, and swim. Meanwhile, Dad kept attending school, which annoyed his father, who said, “Books are a lofty waste of time and money.” His father did not like the idea of higher education; therefore, Dad had to forge his own plan.

He told his father that he would be escorting a few students to a university some three weeks away on foot when he was really escorting himself and not coming back. He walked for weeks in a pair of borrowed shoes. To rest his weary feet, he would stop along the side of the road to brew some tea and eat some bread. To earn money for the tea and bread, he hung a handmade sign that read: Accounting and Letter Writing While You Rest. Every few days, he sat on a rock with a calligrapher’s brush, ink, paper, and an abacus and had no shortage of patrons. Dad had a lot of gumption, conviction, and burning desires that could not be thwarted. The obstacles were many, including the Japanese War and his unsupportive family. When he finally arrived at the university, he was told that the school had closed because of the bombing, but if he walked three weeks west, there was a school that was still running. And so he kept walking.

A person can quickly go from a growth to a fixed mindset just by feeling insecure or defensive when others are critical, or when a challenge feels insurmountable. A fixed mindset can close a person to feedback, cooperation, or owning up to mistakes. In effect, growth can get stifled when we feel vulnerable or shut off. This may also lead to the fear of making mistakes. We will not try new things and will want to avoid failure and criticism. This is the nature of closed-mindedness and fixed thinking.

Attitude and positive thinking certainly help, and the words we use make a difference in how we view learning, growing, and thinking. If we cling to defeatist words (Why do I even try? I cannot win), we will not likely push through the obstacles in life. It’s not a way to learn from lessons that can be instructive and can help us move toward our goals and objectives.

Are You Fired Up?

Wouldn’t it be wonderful if we were all as passionate about our endeavors? My dad had the conviction to plug on—walking for weeks and weeks in a borrowed pair of shoes made from hemp. Imagine what we could accomplish with this sort of zeal and enthusiasm.

How do you get fired up and stay fired up? They say you should do what you love, but that was not the case for Dad. He had planned to get an engineering degree at the first university. Instead, he earned a degree in animal science, the equivalent of veterinary studies, at the second university. It almost didn’t matter what he studied, as long as it was useful, something that would help others, something to help him grow. While Dad had to sweat for his pursuits, he was also a fluid thinker, ready to pivot whenever a situation required. He may have had multiple obstacles in his way, but he also found alternative paths to reach his end goal—of course, that goal kept changing. This kind of fleet-footedness gives hope a chance.

The late psychologist Rick Snyder studied hope, the pursuit of goals, and a diversified perspective and found that a nimble sensibility can help bypass closed doors and see the open ones nearby.

Most people are stuck in the way they think. Yet it doesn’t start that way. Little children happily engage in unrestricted thinking. Alison Gopnik, a professor of psychology at the University of California, Berkeley, and the author of many books, including The Scientist in the Crib, has studied the innate cognitive abilities of children. In one study, she showed adults and children a toy that played music, and everyone was taught how to turn it on by using a set of blocks. The next part of the study entailed turning on the toy with a different set of blocks. The adults mindlessly stuck to their earlier directions, while the children readily discarded prior methods to try new ways to make the toy work.

If we believe our abilities are fixed and go nowhere, they are immutable. If we believe we are capable of moving ahead, then we may just move ahead. Our dedication, curiosity, hard work, and positive outlook may lead us to success. A person with a growth mindset:

  • Puts in the effort to master endeavors

  • Learns and grows from their mistakes

  • Sees challenges and setbacks as opportunities

  • Believes that feedback is good

  • Learns and takes inspiration from others

item.title: Processing Complex Feelings Over a Parent’s Health Decline
item.description:
Caregiving

Processing Complex Feelings Over a Parent’s Health Decline

The healing journey during a parent’s terminal illness or severe health decline.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Complex emotions during a parent's decline include anticipatory grief, regret, and anger.
  • Adult children of an addicted elderly parent have unique challenges during the parent’s decline.
  • Adult daughters may have particular challenges in this journey.
  • Self-care is vital during this time.
Source: LabRobotUIGear/Leonardo.AI

Anticipatory grief, regret, triggering, guilt: All of these and more may be ingredients of the stew of complex emotions swirling around for adult children of a dying parent. For the adult child who grew up in a dysfunctional or addicted family environment, this roller coaster emotional journey can be even more challenging.

Complex Emotions

The lifelong relationship and history between the parent and (now adult) child certainly will impact the emotions the adult child experiences during the parent’s declining health. Certain individuals will experience the anticipatory grief process as bittersweet, especially if the terminally ill parent remains in control of their cognitive faculties. The adult child and parent may take this time to reminisce about happy memories together. For other adult children, the experience is likely to be more complex, especially in the case of a parent with a terminal illness related to an addiction. In those situations, the adult child’s attempts to be supportive while processing anger, resentment, and unforgiveness that surfaces from a traumatic or dysfunctional childhood can make for a turbulent time.

Complex emotions often include anticipatory grief, as well as potentially guilt, regret, unforgiveness, and resentment. During this journey, the adult child may find that surrendering control of this situation can be particularly healthy. The adult child may also begin to face the topic of mortality itself, in their parent and in themself. Additionally, it may be a confusing time for the adult child as they experience role-reversal in caregiving of the declining parent. The bereavement may be more complex in the case of dysfunctional families, including a more ambivalent grieving process as the adult child recalls a far-from-perfect childhood and relationship with the parent.

Anticipatory Grief

Anticipatory grief occurs when we know the parent or loved one will be passing on and we begin processing the grief before they have passed. While anticipatory grief is completely healthy, it may also feel like a double-edged sword. On the one hand, it provides an emotional outlet for the feelings of grief and helplessness for the upcoming loss. On the other hand, though, it’s possible to get mired in the depressed feeling, like falling into a cavern with no visible escape. There are multiple paths out of the cave labyrinth, but it takes commitment to self-care. We need to be committed to consistently pursuing self-care, including reaching out when the feelings become overwhelming or the depression persists.

Adult Daughters

The anticipatory grief process may even be more complex for adult daughters when they are processing emotional pain over the impending loss, particularly when facing the loss of their mother. Adult daughters’ views of their mother, as well as their family and self, may change during this holding-on-letting-go process. Additionally, the daughter may experience adaptation anxiety as she wonders how her mother will adapt to her health decline, as well as anxiety over how she (as the daughter) will adjust and feel after the mother passes on. In fact, adult daughters tend to experience various types of emotional turmoil in caring for dying parents (including emotional, relational, and societal) during this journey of emotional relinquishing.

Addicted or Previously Addicted Aging Parents: A Unique Challenge

A parent’s physical and cognitive decline both carry with them differing challenges for the adult child or loved one. In the case of the elderly person’s physical health problems, deterioration is often clearly visible and obvious. However, alcoholism and serious addiction may not be immediately apparent and may include a whole host of challenges for the adult child or loved one. The adult child may be triggered by the parent’s alcoholism or addiction when it brings up painful childhood memories, as the addiction likely has been a longtime or lifelong challenge for the addicted parent. Providing a balance of empathy while detaching is especially challenging for the adult child when the parent has become elderly and is in serious health decline. Some adult children may find 12-step programs, such as Codependents Anonymous, helpful in this circumstance, while others may find traditional individual or group counseling effective.

In a study examining the challenges of loved ones providing caregiving to an alcoholic family member, several themes were discovered: 1) dealing with emotional peaks and valleys, 2) wandering around in the unknown, 3) an aspect of pointing fingers, 4) riding out the storm, 5) boundaries, and 6) looking back, looking inward. While this study focused on family member caretakers of an alcoholic person, these themes are also likely experienced by various loved ones who provide care to the addicted elderly person in decline.

An added complication may include alcoholic dementia and/or liver failure or other terminal physical condition related to the addiction. In cases in which a parent’s chronic addiction has led to a terminal health condition, adult children have the seemingly overwhelming task of attempting to care for their own emotional well-being when they are triggered while still attempting to assist the parent. Self-care is vital in these situations.

Dementia

Watching a loved one suffer physically can only be matched by the emotional pain of observing a parent’s cognitive or mental decline. In the case of an elderly parent with dementia, the adult child’s emotional pain may be multiplied as they helplessly watch the parent spiral, losing their memory and potentially even displaying disturbing personality changes as they sink deeper into their illness.

When You Cannot Be Present During the Parent’s Health Decline

Remember that we all must travel our own paths, and oftentimes those physical locations don’t coincide with the locations of our parents, relatives, or other loved ones, including during their aging process. Anecdotally, I’ve spoken to many individuals whose aging parents passed on while the adult child lived in another state or country. Many of the adult children were in close daily contact (phone, video calls, texting, etc.) and helped coordinate the care of the declining parent. However, they still felt a certain amount of guilt or regret (even at a less than conscious level) over not being physically present during the parental health decline, including the loved one’s eventual passing. Part of the emotional healing process of releasing feelings of guilt and regret needs to be self-reminders and acceptance that the loved one’s journey was not necessarily the same as our own.

Processing the Pain and Complex Emotions

The healing journey for the adult child includes processing many complex emotions over the death of the parent or loved one and being gentle with oneself.

Remember: No one expects you to be a superhero. Reach out and don’t attempt this alone! Practice self-care and lean on supportive loved ones and counselors.

To find a therapist, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: Back to School, Back to Self!
item.description:
Parenting

Back to School, Back to Self!

How fall routines can create space for parents' identity, career, and recovery

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Fall routines offer parents in recovery an opportunity to reconnect with their identity and personal goals.
  • Maintaining an identity beyond parenthood supports fulfillment, self-worth, and recovery.
  • Work/life/recovery balance requires flexibility and prioritizing recovery alongside family responsibilities.
  • Small, intentional steps can help parents in recovery nurture themselves while supporting their families.

This is the 7th post in the Parents in Recovery series.

Summer can be an opportunity to spend more time together with your family, including vacations, recreational activities, and social events. However, it can also bring disrupted routines, disjointed childcare, overscheduling, and putting personal needs and professional goals on the back burner. As summer ends and children return to school, many parents feel relief as structure returns. For parents in recovery (PIRs) from substance use disorders (SUDs), this transition can provide an opportunity to reassess their own needs, reconnect with their recovery lifestyle, and shift some of their attention toward personal and professional pursuits. For some, this means returning to work with renewed focus. For others, it may involve exploring health and wellness, career changes, educational opportunities, hobbies, volunteering, or simply finding more downtime.

Rediscovering Your Identity Beyond Parenthood

Fall can symbolize the recovery experience—shedding unneeded layers, revealing inner beauty, and letting go of an old life so a new one can grow. When individuals get sober, they organically connect with their core selves and often refocus their lives towards their priorities. At times, parenting can clash with this mission as becoming and continuing to be a parent brings profound personal and professional identity shifts. While many PIRs describe becoming a parent as providing greater meaning and motivation for sobriety, others report struggling to preserve the personal identity they worked so hard to establish.

Cassie, a pharmaceutical researcher and mother, similarly expressed, "I feel I lost the identity that I had found getting sober when I became a parent, and I still struggle with that today."

In contrast, Mason, an EMT and father of three, reports that he has been “Finding greater purpose and fulfillment” since becoming a father.

In her book Why Have Kids? A New Mom Explores the Truth About Parenting and Happiness, Jessica Valenti explores the loss of personal identity that can accompany motherhood, which can also apply to fathers. She describes how the expectations placed on parents can cause their individual interests, accomplishments, and aspirations to become secondary to their parenting role. These experiences highlight the importance of developing a life that includes, but is not entirely defined by, parenting.

The fall return of routines may offer parents an opportunity to reconnect with parts of themselves that have received less attention during the summer.

Work, Purpose, and Personal Fulfillment

Historical context can help to understand how gender roles have shifted over time. Traditional male and female roles were affected by the increase in women attaining education and entering the labor force in the second half of the 20th century—specifically from the 1960s through the 1980s. Following the women’s rights movement, the proportion of women who pursued a college degree quadrupled, while the proportion of men doubled, from 1970 to 2021.

In 2020, 57% of women worked full-time compared with just 40.7% in 1970. The workforce has evened out, and this has led both mothers and fathers to wrestle with career identity and fulfillment. For some PIRs, these pursuits may also strengthen the positive identity and self-worth developed in recovery.

Claire, an occupational therapist and mother, described the importance of her career in early sobriety, stating, "I leaned into my career and motherhood, and I felt like it gave me a sense of purpose, a role that brought me dignity and self-worth."

Other parents found that as their children became more independent, they had greater flexibility to explore new opportunities. Jake, a business owner and father of a young girl, expresses, “Being a parent created the largest shift in my life. The connection that has been made between my daughter and my wife, and me is overwhelming. It’s hard to explain how I changed, but I became a man.

Finding Work/Life/Recovery Balance

Of course, the return to fall structure does not magically eliminate competing demands. School schedules, extracurricular activities, professional responsibilities, and household obligations can quickly fill the time that summer once occupied. When PIRs were asked how they had found work/life/recovery balance, their responses included, "Balance is elusive,” "There is no balance. It's hard,” "Still working on it!" These responses capture the reality that balance is not a fixed destination but an ongoing process of adjustment.

For PIRs, an additional challenge involves maintaining their recovery identity while managing parenting and professional responsibilities. During busy periods, recovery meetings, therapy, social connections, and self-care can gradually become less frequent. However, these activities are not luxuries that should only occur when everything else is accomplished.

Liz Modugno, LCSW, LADC, encourages PIRs to reframe the belief that "meetings and therapy take away from my kids and family" into "meetings and therapy give me and my children a sober and healthy life together." This perspective can also apply to other meaningful personal pursuits. Parents who nurture their interests, relationships, and professional identities are not necessarily taking something away from their families.

The following are some suggestions for reclaiming your time, balance, and identity this fall:

Reconnect with your personal identity:

  • Identify interests, hobbies, or goals that are independent of your parenting role.
  • Consider what brought you fulfillment before having children and what new interests have emerged in recovery.
  • Put some amount of time into something that brings YOU joy.

Reassess your personal and professional goals:

  • Identify a life domain you would like to prioritize this fall, such as career, education, personal growth, spirituality, or creative pursuits.
  • Establish realistic short-term and long-term goals that fit your current family circumstances.
  • Take small steps rather than waiting for the ideal opportunity or schedule.

Create structure without rigidity:

  • Develop a weekly routine that includes dedicated time for parenting, work, recovery, and personal interests.
  • Consider using a shared family calendar to organize responsibilities.
  • Examine how you are spending your time and whether it aligns with your priorities.
  • Allow flexibility as family needs and circumstances change.

Keep recovery integrated into your lifestyle:

  • Re-establish recovery meetings, therapy, or other supports that may have been disrupted during the summer.
  • Maintain social connections with other PIRs.
  • Schedule small pockets of personal time, even if they begin with just a few minutes.

While the fall transition can mean the end of the warmer months, it can also provide an opportunity for parents to consider what they want this fresh season to look like.

item.title: Why AI Can Know Your Interests but Miss Your Feelings
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Why AI Can Know Your Interests but Miss Your Feelings

Messages can reflect what you want without resolving your ambivalence.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Personalized messages can identify what attracts us without revealing what makes us hesitate.
  • Ambivalence often means weighing a desired gain against something we fear losing.
  • Framing can shift decisions by emphasizing gains or losses even when the options stay the same.
  • More information may not resolve uncertainty when the real conflict is between priorities.
When a message feels personal, consider what it captures and what it leaves out.
Source: Image by Pexels from Pixabay

Personalized messages may reflect what we want without addressing why we hesitate.

You have been looking at a course that could help your career. Soon, advertisements appear in your feed. They mention skills you want to develop, describe opportunities in your industry, and suggest that your next chapter is within reach. The messages seem relevant. You still do not sign up.

Perhaps you want to progress but feel exhausted by the prospect of proving yourself again. Perhaps you are interested in leadership but reluctant to lose the parts of your job you enjoy. The course offers a clear next step when you are uncertain whether you want to continue in that direction.

The message recognizes an interest. The decision involves a conflict.

Marketing entrepreneur Furkat Kasimov, founder of AppLayerAI, argues that AI marketing would benefit from greater attention to the psychology behind consumer decisions. His perspective raises a useful question: How much does recognizing someone’s interests tell us about what makes choosing difficult?

Personalized communication can feel accurate and incomplete at the same time. What attracts our attention does not necessarily reveal the competing feelings that make acting on that interest difficult.

We Can Want Something And Resist It

Imagine two people researching the same qualification. Both compare fees, explore the syllabus, and read graduate testimonials. One feels excited about a promotion. The other worries about being left behind.

Even those descriptions may be too simple. The excited person might also fear becoming responsible for other people’s performance. The worried person might resent the expectation of constantly acquiring new skills. Each could be moving toward something desirable while trying to protect something already valued.

This is ambivalence: holding conflicting feelings or evaluations about the same possibility. In these examples, hesitation makes sense. Progress could bring opportunity, but it could also threaten time, confidence, or a familiar professional identity.

A message that addresses only the appealing side may leave the difficult part untouched. More encouragement to advance does little to resolve uncertainty about what advancement would cost.

AI can incorporate psychological information. Research has demonstrated the potential for large language models to generate personalized persuasive messages based on recipients’ characteristics. That does not establish that a particular message has accurately identified someone’s conflicting motives.

A useful question is: “What do I want here, and what am I reluctant to give up?” Both answers deserve attention.

The Message Selects Part Of The Story

Consider two ways to describe that course: “Prepare for your next opportunity” and “Keep your skills from becoming outdated.” The first brings a possible gain into view. The second highlights something that might be lost.

Kasimov’s argument emphasizes how a message frames a choice. The psychological question extends beyond whether that framing attracts a response: Which concern does it bring into focus, and which considerations remain unaddressed?

Research on decision framing showed that preferences between risky and certain options could shift when equivalent outcomes were described in terms of gains or losses. Presentation can influence judgment even when the underlying possibilities remain unchanged.

This does not establish that warnings always persuade more effectively than encouragement. It invites us to notice which interpretation a message encourages. Are we considering an opportunity, defending against a threat, or trying to avoid anticipated regret?

An advertisement about outdated skills might resonate with an existing worry. Resonance alone does not tell us whether that worry is proportionate or whether the course would address it.

Try describing the choice without the advertisement’s language. What would change if you accepted? What would remain unresolved? What might you gain by declining?

Sometimes We Need Priorities Before Options

A difficult decision can look like an information problem. We keep searching because another detail might finally make the answer obvious.

Sometimes it does. But imagine choosing between two jobs when one offers greater status and the other offers more time at home. Additional facts may help, yet the central question could remain: What matters most at this point in your life?

Kasimov also highlights choice overload as a consideration in designing AI marketing messages. That is a useful starting point, although reducing the number of options does not necessarily resolve uncertainty about what someone wants.

Research cautions against simple rules. A meta-analysis of choice overload found an average effect close to zero across the included experiments, alongside considerable variation. More options are not uniformly harmful; their effects depend on the circumstances.

The practical distinction is between needing to know more about the alternatives and needing to understand your priorities. Personalized recommendations may help with the former while leaving the latter open.

Before requesting another list, ask what information could realistically change your decision. You may discover a trade-off that further searching cannot resolve.

Feeling Recognized Is a Starting Point

Communication that reflects our interests can introduce possibilities we have overlooked or help us put a concern into words. But recognizing one part of our experience does not resolve the rest.

“You want to progress” may be true alongside “You need a period of stability.” A useful decision needs room for both.

When a message feels personal, consider what it captures and what it leaves out. Its recommendation may fit. Your hesitation may also contain information the message never asked for.

Sometimes the most helpful next step is to understand what makes saying yes difficult.

item.title: Feeling Your Way to Change With Experiential Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

Feeling Your Way to Change With Experiential Therapy

Experiential therapy approaches work by targeting implicit emotional memories.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Conscious reasoning isn't always enough to change ingrained emotional beliefs and patterns.
  • Experiential therapies provide opportunities that challenge what your mind and body have come to expect.
  • Disconfirming emotional experiences update the nervous system, allowing for new feelings to take root.

If you're an over thinker or have previously been to therapy, you may understand your patterns and even know why you feel the way you do. However, this insight alone may not be enough to fully change how you feel about your situation.

This can be such a frustrating experience. So why does this happen?

You can intellectually understand your fears, beliefs, or lived experiences come from the past or are irrational, yet your nervous system continues to respond as if the threat is happening in the present. These reactions are due to implicit emotional memories, or emotional learnings that your body stores when the experience is overwhelming or unable to be processed fully.

How Bottom-Up Therapies Work With Implicit Memories

Experiential approaches, such as Accelerated Experiential Dynamic Psychotherapy (AEDP), Coherence Therapy, Emotion-Focused Therapy (EFT), Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR), Intensive Short-Term Dynamic Psychotherapy (ISTDP), Internal Family Systems (IFS), and Somatic Experiencing (SE), all have one thing in common: They move beyond intellectual insight to work directly with emotional experience.

Instead of staying in perpetual analysis, therapists trained in these modalities help clients notice and explore the physical sensations, beliefs, images, and protective responses associated with their emotional learning. While they use different techniques, each provides a way of working in the moment with emotional learning that goes beyond simply talking or explaining it.

This might involve fully experiencing an emotion that was previously avoided, noticing or following sensations and impulses in the body, or having a new emotional experience that contradicts what the person has learned to expect. In experiential therapy, the body becomes part of the therapeutic process. This is key because, contrary to what most people believe, emotions aren't psychological events; they're something we experience physiologically.

How the Brain Learns Through Emotional Experience

Consider an individual who struggles with people-pleasing and caretaking, yet may be aware of the origins of this pattern. They may feel frustrated by their inability to set boundaries, assert themselves, or communicate their needs, leading to self-criticism and increasing resentment and dissatisfaction in their relationships. When this pattern emerges in therapy, the therapist may help the client to have a new, corrective emotional experience of getting their own needs met, due to not having to take care of the therapist, while also processing the underlying grief, anger, and hurt at the cost of such prior self-abandonment. This type of therapeutic experience can activate the brain's capacity to form new pathways and update old emotional learning so that change becomes felt and integrated — a phenomenon known as neuroplasticity.

This type of emotional experience can have a profound impact on the individual's former narrative of abandoning oneself in order to care for others. Oftentimes, what we see in therapy is that a maladaptive belief system (e.g., "I must put the needs of others first, even at my own expense") is never directly challenged. Instead, when a person has an experience that contradicts what their nervous system has learned to expect, the old belief may naturally lose its emotional hold. What emerges is a new, more self-empowered belief or insight that arises organically and is experienced by the individual as compelling and true. In this example, the individual may genuinely feel "My needs matter" because they had the felt experience that expressing their needs or preferences didn't lead to the anticipated rejection, shaming, conflict, or loss of connection they'd learned to anticipate.

Therapeutic Impact and Benefit

A meta-analysis found that clients who engaged more deeply in processing and making meaning from their internal experiences during therapy had better treatment outcomes, suggesting that experiential engagement may be a common factor in effective psychotherapy. Additionally, a meta-analysis of 57 randomized controlled trials involving 4,300 participants found that experiential dynamic therapies (a family of affect-focused approaches that includes AEDP and ISTDP) produced significant and sustained improvements across anxiety, mood, personality, and somatic disorders.

Over time or suddenly, new emotional learning can influence how people interact with the world outside of the therapy room. Unlike top-down approaches, like Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) or Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT), which emphasize challenging unhelpful cognitions or implementing coping skills to bring about change, the person with difficulty expressing their needs won't have to consciously remind themselves to set a boundary or reason their way out of a thought. They may simply find that asserting themselves feels more natural, or that they feel less inhibited by guilt or anxiety to act on their needs.

Ultimately, sustained therapeutic change for more ingrained patterns isn't just about learning a more adaptive way to think. Experiential therapies can help people embody new emotional experiences that allow the nervous system to respond differently when familiar situations arise.

item.title: 6 Tactics From Domestic Abusers’ Litigation Playbook
item.description:
Domestic Violence

6 Tactics From Domestic Abusers’ Litigation Playbook

Post-separation, abusers control and intimidate victims through family court.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Domestic abusers may employ litigation tactics to continue abusing through the courts.
  • Abusers often try to portray their victims as crazy, addicted, violent, and "high-conflict."
  • Claims of "mutual abuse" and "parental alienation" confuse the courts and distract from real dangers.
  • Prolonged abusive litigation puts adult and child survivors at risk.

This piece is co-authored by Lisa Aronson Fontes, Ph.D., and Jenny Wiggs, Ed.D.

When they leave an abusive relationship, domestic violence survivors believe the hardest part is over. They expect family court will protect them and their children. It can be a shock to discover that the abuse dynamics have morphed but not ceased. Domineering tactics now unfold through pleadings, motions, custody evaluations, discovery, and courtroom proceedings.

Across jurisdictions, survivors report similar litigation narratives that undermine their credibility, cast doubt on their parenting, diminish their finances, and distort the past. Recognizing these patterns can help survivors and those who work with them respond strategically instead of reactively.

1. Pathologizing the Survivor: “Crazy and Addicted”

Abusers and their attorneys try to pathologize the survivor as mentally ill, substance-abusing, or both. Abusers often describe survivors as anxious, unstable, depressed, paranoid, dysregulated, irrational, and incapable of making sound decisions. Courts focus on the victim’s alleged shortcomings and away from true abuse.

Abusers, their attorneys, and the mental health professionals they hire often apply serious psychiatric labels to victims. Favorites include bipolar, borderline, paranoid, or histrionic personality disorders and even psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia or delusional disorders. Abusers often weaponize normative experiences such as postpartum depression or maternal anxiety to portray the survivor as permanently unfit for parenting.

This litigation strategy is effective because it exploits a survivor’s abuse-induced trauma. After prolonged abuse, many survivors experience post-traumatic stress symptoms (Fernandez-Fillol, 2021). These merit compassion; they should not be weaponized in custody litigation. Seeking treatment for trauma is evidence of resilience—not parental unfitness.

The psychological tests used by custody evaluators often obscure more than they illuminate. Instruments such as the MMPI were not designed as stand-alone measures of parenting capacity. Likewise, diagnosing complex psychiatric conditions requires careful clinical evaluation over time, incorporating several sources of information. No single test score, isolated interview, or litigation narrative should be mistaken for a comprehensive psychiatric diagnosis or a definitive assessment of a person’s ability to parent.

When the “crazy” label fails to stick, domestic abusers often allege that the victim abuses drugs or alcohol. Survivors sometimes undergo years of substance abuse testing, at great expense and inconvenience. And even if their tests never come up positive for a substance, the testing period may be extended if they are early or late for a test. This is ironic because often the domestic abuser has a true problem with alcohol or drug abuse. Whoever flings the first allegation catches the judge’s attention.

2. Alleging Alienation: “Turned the Kids Against Me”

Abusers often allege that the protective parent—usually the mother—is “alienating” the children. Domestic abuse survivors are accused of manipulating children’s perceptions, exaggerating abuse concerns, or intentionally damaging children’s relationship with the other parent. Alienation allegations are a litigation strategy that has no basis in science (Birchall & Choudhry, 2022).

Children become estranged from parents for many reasons (Mercer, 2025). Children fear parents who have acted abusively toward them or their other parent. They dislike parents who lack warmth. Abuse allegations shouldn’t be dismissed simply because the alleged perpetrator has waved the flag of parental alienation.

3. Claiming Mutual Abuse: “Both Hot-Headed”

When domestic abusers cannot disprove abuse, they claim the relationship was characterized by mutual abuse or “two-way domestic violence.” This reframing shifts the conversation away from power and control patterns toward isolated conflicts. Rather than examining who exercised coercive control, the focus narrows to moments when the survivor resisted domination. Abusers claim, “We both yelled and cursed” or “We had a lot of conflict.”

This is a form of DARVO—Deny, Attack, and Reverse Victim and Offender (Platt et al., 2009). Rather than acknowledging abusive conduct, the abuser deflects responsibility and blames the victim. Survivors’ emotional responses and efforts to protect themselves or their children, establish boundaries, or document abuse are presented as “evidence” that the victim was equally abusive. Domestic abusers provoke and record their victims, then use edited recordings to portray the victim as “the problem” or claim “mutual abuse.”

We must distinguish reactive behavior from abuse. Victims don’t always respond ideally. They may yell, curse, send angry messages, or respond emotionally after prolonged intimidation, surveillance, or violence. These reactions must be viewed within their broader context rather than in isolation. The legal question is not whether a survivor ever became angry. Rather, the question is whether one party engaged in a sustained pattern of domination that reduced the other person’s autonomy and made them afraid.

The courts should be helped to reject false equivalencies so coercive control is understood for what it is: one partner’s campaign to dominate the other.

4. Confusing High Conflict and Litigation Abuse

Abusers and their legal teams often rely on “high-conflict” narratives to deflect from holding the abuser accountable. As a result, judges and evaluators may struggle to understand the true power and control dynamics and the associated risk for adult and child survivors. Conflict and coercive control are not synonymous. Conflict generally involves two people who both escalate a dispute. Coercive control, in contrast, involves one individual systematically dominating the other. Failing to distinguish between the two results in erroneous decisions.

Domestic abuse survivors usually try mightily to pacify their abusive partners and de-escalate abuse. Nevertheless, courts may label them as “high conflict” along with the abuser. The designation often follows predictable events: the survivor reports abuse, requests financial disclosures, objects to inappropriate parenting, rejects unsafe arrangements, or seeks enforcement of court orders. Actions that are intended to establish accountability are reframed as evidence that the survivor is unable to co-parent or unwilling to compromise.

5. Attacking Maternal Identity: “Bad Mom”

After separation, many domestic abusers try to cast their victims as inadequate or abusive parents. They often call child protective services with false allegations and sometimes are able to fulfill their threat to “take away the kids” or limit the survivor to supervised or video visits only.

Many women endure unfathomable abuse “for the sake of the children.” Abused mothers often protect their children, shield them from violence, manage the home, attend medical appointments, help with homework, comfort crying children, and carry the emotional labor of parenting. Eventually, they may leave the relationship to protect the children. It is psychologically devastating to have those years of devotion recast as evidence of neglect, failure to protect, or enmeshment.

6. Abusing Through Endless Litigation

Perhaps the most damaging family court litigation strategy involves wearing down the survivor. Cases drag on for years. The survivor runs out of funds for legal support. The process itself becomes the mechanism through which coercive control continues.

The cumulative effects are profound. Survivors sometimes endure more than a decade of financial impoverishment and extreme stress as the other parent files motion after baseless motion while refusing to follow court orders. Every motion requires a response. Every expert requires payment. Every delay prolongs uncertainty.

Abusers’ twin goals are to maintain contact with the survivor through litigation and to increase legal costs until the survivor gives up. Survivors may accept inequitable property divisions because they cannot afford more litigation. They may agree to unsafe parenting arrangements because they lack the emotional capacity to keep fighting.

Abusers’ Litigation Narratives Are Dangerous

Abusers’ litigation narratives disparaging the survivor confuse the court and obscure real risks. We give the final words here to Leah Moses, a nurse-midwife who tried to protect her children in court for 12 years after separating from her psychologist husband.

Court evaluators catalogued my protective parenting behaviors as “high conflict,” “custodial interference,” and “alienating.” My warnings of escalating risk were dismissed or drowned out by combative court hearings and mediations, invasive evaluations, and conflicting court orders.

Family court became my ex-husband’s instrument of control…. One of the biggest mistakes we make is assuming that dangerous people look dangerous.”

Moses’s ex-husband shot and killed their teenage son and then himself. Utah’s amended bill on child safety in custody proceedings is named after Moses’s son, Om.

item.title: You Can Change Your Thinking and Still Feel Lost
item.description:
Cognitive Behavioral Therapy

You Can Change Your Thinking and Still Feel Lost

Knowing what is true does not alway tell us what to do.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Therapy often stresses thinking differently about challenges you face. That can be helpful but not enough.
  • Looking at things differently does not tell you what to do with the reality of what you find.
  • Questioning what reality tells you about what you are facing can help you address deeper issues.
  • These issues include what you find meaningful and why you want to bother changing in the first place.

Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), arguably the most common approach to psychotherapy, rests on the powerful premise that “how we think about a problem affects how we feel about it.”

And that premise makes sense. Change how you interpret a problem, and you will change how you feel about it.

But what happens when the distressing thoughts are actually true? What happens when recognizing reality also means accepting something negative about reality?

Here’s an example. Someone thinks other people do not like them. CBT might emphasize that the person could be misinterpreting this situation. Maybe they are misinterpreting cues as evidence that people do not like them. Or maybe there is little likelihood that people are thinking about them at all.

Not bad alternatives. But what if the reality is that people do not actually like them? Or what if the reality of people not even thinking about them is by itself distressing?

These are truths about life that can cause their own level of difficulty. Because what do you do with that information? What do you do when evidence suggests that people do not like you? Or that you are not important enough for them to even think about you?

If the way we interpret things contributes to our emotional problems, then changing how we think about those things should help us respond differently. But what happens when you learn to think about things differently and still don’t know what to do with that information?

Here’s another example. A person may reach the point where they are able to think differently about work situations and draw a different conclusion: “I know that my boss’s criticism doesn’t mean I’m a worthless person.”

And that is helpful. But then the multiple other questions come up, like “Should I stay at this job or leave it?” “Should I confront my boss?” “Am I only staying at this job because it provides security?”

CBT focuses on asking, “Is this thought accurate?” But living a full life also requires asking, “Given what is true, what should I do?” Answering that question is important for moving beyond just the basics of what CBT offers.

Thinking more rationally helps us get closer to seeing reality as it actually is. But that actually creates another problem. What do we do with that reality once we see it more clearly?

Knowing what is true does not by itself help us know what to do next. Other factors, gathered from animal and human psychology research, that impact what an individual does with new information include motivation, prior learning, and change avoidance (Pisula, 2025).

Here are some examples of other factors that impact how we act even when we are able to think differently about situations:

  • “I know why change would help here; it just isn’t worth the effort” (motivation)
  • “Things are OK right now. Not great, but OK. Why risk changing that?” (change avoidance)
  • “I have tried to change before, but nothing happened. Why would I think this time would be any different?” (prior learning)
  • “What I learned helps me see reality more clearly. But that doesn’t mean I can change it.” (acceptance)

Notice that each of these statements reflects a strong recognition of reality. And notice that they are not necessarily bad. In fact, the issue of acceptance can be a big part of moving forward in CBT. “Radical acceptance” in therapy is often very useful for helping a person recognize reality and live with it, even if it is not positive.

What each of these factors has in common is that they require the person to take another step beyond changing their thinking. This requires them to address not only how they view what is happening around them but what that reality says about how they want to live their life.

Doing this requires asking questions deeper than just “What do I think about this?” These questions include:

  • “Do I really want to change, or am I saying I want to change because I think that I’m supposed to want to change?”
  • “Does how I am now fit with the sort of person I want to be? If it does, then why do I need to change even if other people are not happy with it?”
  • “What do I really find meaningful in life? Is making a change going to move me in that direction? If not, is it really that important?”
  • “Do I know anything about why my prior attempts to change didn’t help? What does that say about what I am really looking for from changing?”

These are questions that are less about how the person sees specific situations and more about understanding what the person wants from life. They are still in the realm of CBT but just in a deeper realm. Here, change moves from asking questions about specific situations to asking questions about meaning and purpose. These are questions that help a person move from just living a more positive life to living a more meaningful life.

item.title: Schizophrenia Made Me a Better Person
item.description:
Friends

Schizophrenia Made Me a Better Person

Personal Perspective: Today I am more well-rounded and compassionate than I was before schizophrenia.

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • In high school, I was too competitive and not very social.
  • In college, things were perfect. I was living in the dorm and taking classes I loved. But I was not happy.
  • A humanitarian trip to Africa radically changed my life, helping me find compassion and friendship.
  • Today I am more family-oriented and well-rounded than I ever was before schizophrenia interrupted my life.
View from our condo at the beach
Source: Bethany Yeiser

I was recently recording a podcast with a producer who asked me the following question: Has schizophrenia changed who you are as a person?

I was so surprised by his question. I am not sure I ever considered how schizophrenia has changed me over time. But with some thought, I now realize that it has changed me significantly, and most surprisingly, I would say it has changed me for the better.

Reflections on a Family Vacation

Last week, I spent five days on the coast of North Carolina in a rented condo with my mom and dad. We used to go every summer when I was growing up, usually spending a week at a small house we rented on the ocean called “Two Gulls.” In more recent years, we have rented a condo on the ocean instead, as it also has a swimming pool only yards away from the beach.

As we spent our week swimming in the pool, walking the ocean, collecting shells and wading through the waves, I felt perfectly happy. It was so fun to spend this special time with my parents, and I had forgotten just how well both of them cook.

But the biggest surprise to me was the difference between how I felt on the beach in 2026 versus how I felt when we vacationed there when I was in high school.

When I was in high school, I had everything going for me. I was taking college classes for dual high school and college credit and getting straight A’s. I had a beautiful violin and a position with the Cleveland Orchestra Youth Orchestra. My violin teacher was one of the best in the country.

But I was not happy. In fact, I found myself grieving. All I wanted was to be a touring violin soloist, and despite practicing four to five hours a day throughout the year all the way through high school, I was not one of the best of the best.

Throughout the whole year, and even when I was on a vacation that was supposed to make me happy, it was as though everything in my life had gone wrong, as I had not reached my lofty goals. I took the violin along on vacation and chose to practice when I could have been walking the beach.

How Schizophrenia Shaped My College Experience

As I was finishing high school, I became a national merit scholar and designated the University of Southern California as my first choice school. I wanted to study violin there with another famous violin professor.

But when I toured USC, I was amazed by the opportunities everywhere. I realized I could become an engineer, a biochemist, or a physicist. The career possibilities seemed endless.

When I was not accepted by this California violin teacher, it was OK with me. I was determined to attend USC and major in science and/or engineering.

As I moved into the USC honors dormitory, signed up for classes and began to live the college life I had been dreaming of for years, things were still not okay. The sadness that I had felt in high school would not go away. Even as I embarked on this whole new life, I was still grieving. There really wasn’t a reason why.

My parents sacrificed everything to help me pay for USC. But I had little interest in speaking with them. Every morning, the girls in the dorm would get together to have breakfast together, but I joined them only once or twice my entire first semester. I found the dorm had an upstairs attic and would often sit there alone.

As my relationships deteriorated, my grades did as well. I remember an inability to concentrate in a biochemistry class that would have been easy for me years back. When I scored a B in the class, I hated myself for it and became even more upset.

My life at USC in the dorm, surrounded by high achieving students and with lots of opportunities for clubs and activities, should have been perfect. But I was not happy.

I remember the second semester of my sophomore year at USC when I got my life together. I scored A’s in advanced biochemistry and engineering physics and a B in differential equations (I wonder to this day if I would've gotten straight A’s had I been at my best). But this success was short lived. As I started my junior year, my grades dropped again, and I couldn’t concentrate. That semester, I scored C’s. When I had entered USC, the dream was to scored straight A’s. I felt like a failure, which affected my ability to concentrate even more.

The summer after my junior year of college, I made one of the best decisions of my life. I left the competition and the potential for awards and achieving success back in California and spent two months in Africa. While I was there, I connected with kind people living in the Nairobi slums who I quickly came to love. I realized there was more to life than straight A’s, and that relationships are really the most important aspect of our lives.

My schizophrenia hit when I returned from Africa. I would drop out of college, paranoid of my family and all of my friends, and become homeless in the LA area for four years. I would spend another year hopeless, looking desperately for an effective medication. This followed a difficult involuntary psychiatric commitment. It was hard, and I suffered, but I made it through.

What Recovery From Schizophrenia Taught Me

Today, in recovery, I am happy. Life is not about scoring straight A’s or winning competitions on violin or academic awards. I have been content with my life since 2009 when I was able to return to college and graduate in molecular biology with nearly straight A’s, a functional, mind and many close friends.

Today, I am very close with my family again and many friends in the Cincinnati area. I am fulfilled running my nonprofit foundation for schizophrenia education and advocacy, which I cofounded with my doctor in 2016. Above all, I recognize that I am happy. Perhaps I have schizophrenia to thank for that.

item.title: Three Paradigms of Living
item.description:
Self-Help

Three Paradigms of Living

From contentment to resilience to meaning, which one resonates most with you?

Posted October 2, 2026

Key points
  • Everyone chooses their own path to fulfillment, guided by their unique life paradigm.
  • The will to find meaning comes from within.
  • How are you choosing to explore your true self?
Source: Elisa Riva / Pixabay

Of course, we want to enjoy life and, at the end of our lives, feel satisfied with our choices and how we ultimately lived.

Everyone chooses their own path to fulfillment, guided by their unique life paradigm. A paradigm is defined as a framework of beliefs, values, and ideas that filter how you see the world. Your paradigm influences your choices and shapes your life.

There are numerous life paradigms ranging from a nihilistic perspective, which focuses on the meaninglessness of life and distrust of others, to a more introspective approach, focused on the search for deeper meaning.

In this article, I offer three paradigms for consideration. Reflect on which one may be central to how you are choosing to live your life.

The Contentment Paradigm

The state of being content is often defined as a state of calmness, ease, and acceptance of one’s situation in life. This approach can help one feel safe and secure while dealing with an uncertain world. It can also help one avoid the constant comparison with the lives (and possessions) of others, which can often lead to feelings of dissatisfaction with one’s own life, low self-esteem, and unhappiness.

However, when someone says, “I hope you find contentment,” it can be misinterpreted as a judgment call that their life is superior to how you are living your life. They may believe they are recommending that you choose a life that is “safer” and “more settled,” often guided and judged by their needs, value choices, and fears, not yours.

The weakness with seeking contentment is that dissatisfaction with life is actually necessary and beneficial for learning, growth, and self-discovery. For example, feeling weak stimulates one to strengthen one’s body through exercise; feeling out of place causes one to seek new circumstances that resonate closer to one’s heart; misunderstanding the world causes one to open one’s mind to learn new concepts, etc.

If you are reaching the retirement age of 60+, reflect on how your life choices have evolved. Are you choosing a life that feels like it is expanding or a life that feels routine, contracting, or even atrophying? This question goes beyond the “bucket list” question of activities one might want to experience in their later years to the deeper, more existential question: “How are you choosing to explore your true self in your latter years?”

The Resilience Paradigm

Life cannot be preprogrammed, for it flows like a river, twisting and turning, changing at different rates, sometimes appearing more stable, while at other times, like right now, tossing us around in the turbulent rapids. Indeed, life is change, but we often resist it, wanting things to stay the same and trying to design and control our lives so change doesn’t happen.

We think that if we stay in the same house, work in the same place at the same job, and keep the same friends, we’ll be able to avoid having to deal with change. But the status quo is an illusion because, even if we want to stand still, everyone and everything else around us is changing.

As the ancient Greek philosopher Heraclitus advised, life is always in flux, situations are changing, and a new approach to living may be needed. Choosing a resilience paradigm can help you prepare for and thrive during difficult times, such as political conflicts, changing rules, inflation, famine, loss of financial wealth, weather, fires, accidents—all the things in life that are mostly outside your power of influence.

Resilience involves believing that you can make things better for yourself versus being a helpless victim of your circumstances. As the world-famous psychiatrist Dr. Viktor Frankl taught us, it is not about what happens to us, but how we react that really matters.1 If you are resilient, you can recover more quickly and adapt to new situations. You can choose how you think and feel, as well as what you do.

The Meaning Paradigm

Viktor Frankl discovered during World War II that having a sense of meaning was the most important determinant of survival. But he observed, “Even more people today have the means to live but no meaning to live for.” 2

We can find meaning in any given moment, and we can also find meaning when we step back and reflect on the overall state of our lives. In my book, The OPA! Way,3 I offer an easy-to-understand formula for finding meaning in three elements of our life: connecting meaningfully with others (O); engaging with deeper purpose and positively impacting the world (P); and embracing all of life, including our health, with a positive attitude (A).

Ask yourself, “What is most important in my life, and how can I put these meaningful elements at the core of my life each day?” Remember, the will to meaning comes from within. It comes from having a deep resonance with who you are at your core, beyond your tasks, roles, titles, money, or possessions. Having a deeper understanding of yourself—knowing yourself and knowing your sources of meaning—will help you weather the storms that come your way.

Everyone has their own paradigm for how they want to live and seek fulfillment: some choose to be motivated by contentment, some choose resilience, and others choose meaning. Choose what works for you…and remember, try to avoid choosing a life paradigm for others. It is their life and their choice as well!
